CMS Prevents $1.6 Billion in Fraudulent Medicare Laboratory Payments
157 lab providers kicked out of Medicare.

That is not a rounding error. That is a pipeline.
Since President Trump returned to office, CMS and the White House Task Force to Eliminate Fraud have blocked or clawed back more than $1.6 billion in potentially improper Medicare laboratory payments. 

The labs were billing for tests that were never performed, tests patients did not need, and services marked up beyond what should have been paid.

Here is how the $1.6 billion breaks down.
$732 million saved by revoking 157 fraudulent lab providers from the Medicare program.
More than $500 million stopped after investigators reviewed about 600 labs and issued 185 payment suspensions.
$276 million recouped from 442 overpayments that had already gone out the door.
$127 million prevented after 85 cases were referred to law enforcement.
Read that again. Some of the money never left. Some of it had to be chased after it was already stolen. Both are an admission that the system was being farmed.

One case shows how easy it was. A consulting-company owner enrolled 14 laboratories in Medicare and billed more than $24 million. CMS said none of those labs appeared to be operating. No working clinic. No staff. No equipment. Fourteen names on paper and a claim machine aimed at the Trust Fund. CMS held back $12 million, recovered another $7 million, and removed most of those labs from the program. The rest are still under investigation.

That is not health care. That is a billing operation wearing a lab coat.

CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz said the obvious part out loud. When laboratories bill Medicare for tests they never performed, it drains the Medicare Trust Fund and diverts resources away from beneficiaries who need them. Under the White House Anti-Fraud Task Force, CMS says it has built a technology-powered operation using analytics and machine-learning models to flag suspicious patterns before the check goes out. Genetic tests. Drug tests. Pathogen panels. Claims for patients who had no relationship with the ordering provider. Empty offices billing like they were running a hospital.
This did not start last week. CMS launched the Fraud Defense Operations Center in 2025. Agency figures put overall Medicare fraud-prevention savings at $42 billion in fiscal year 2025. So far in fiscal year 2026, CMS says it has identified $1.8 billion in Medicare overpayments, collected $378 million, and suspended hundreds of millions more in suspected fraud across labs, medical equipment, hospice, and other corners of the program.
The White House line was blunt. The previous administration treated taxpayer-funded programs as piggy banks for fraudsters.

Seniors paid into Medicare their entire working lives. They were told the money would be there when they needed a real test, a real diagnosis, a real doctor. Instead a chunk of it was being vacuumed out by operations that never drew blood, never ran a machine, and never saw the patient.

Fraud is not compassion. It is theft from the people who can least afford it.
Revoke the fake labs. Suspend the payments. Refer the cases. Keep the Trust Fund for Americans who actually earned it.
This is what enforcement looks like when someone decides the scam is no longer the cost of doing business.

@elonmusk has said that humanoid robots “will probably be worth significantly more than the car side of things long-term."

Have you ever wondered how much more?

Let’s take a look at Tesla’s humanoid robot opportunity.

... Introducing the Boundless Optimus Transformation at Scale "BOTS" Model for Tesla.

This model only considers the potential value of Tesla's Optimus humanoid robot when made at scale. Note: I say "potential" - as this isn't a company valuation model and these are not predictions - the purpose is simply to show "what if"

The BOTS model shows rather astounding what if values – as every bot produced, could add about $380,000 to Tesla’s market value. 

100 million bots could add $38 trillion.

If you think this sounds crazy, take a look at how I arrive at these numbers...

The assumptions:

1) Tesla does not sell bots. Instead they lease them. This gives Tesla control over how people use them – after all we don’t want anyone building their own robot army!

2) The bots monthly lease cost varies based on their capabilities, wear and tear, and risk of damage, but the average monthly lease is $3,600. If the bot works 16 hours per day, that’s an effective hourly “labor” cost of only $7.50.

3) The BOTS model excludes all other revenue from Auto, FSD, Autonomy, Energy, Insurance, Supercharging, Service, and Dojo.

4) The cost to make a bot is $15,000, they last ten years, but annual maintenance and repair costs equal 12.5% or $1,875 per year, bringing the lifetime cost of each bot to $33,750.

5) There is a ROBot tax of 33% of bot revenue. As humanoid bots displace workers in factories and outside, governments are likely to lose a lot of tax revenue. In the US lost payroll taxes and taxes that support Social Security, Medicare and Unemployment Insurance programs could be partially recouped with a ROBot tax.

6) Net profit margins are 29%. Note: the government would generate more tax revenue from each BOT than Tesla makes in profit. In addition to lots of tax revenue, governments should love bots as they don’t have to pay them unemployment benefits, workers compensation claims, Social Security benefits or worry about healthcare costs. Bots could be a significant part of a solution to saving government entitlement programs like Social Security, Medicare, Medicaid, Unemployment and welfare. Bots also help to address a shortage of labor, particularly in countries with low birth rates.

7) Investors give the company a P/E multiple of 30 for steady, growing, high margin earnings. None of the numbers in the model are discounted to the present as there are no implied time frames.

The model's results:

Each bot generates $43,200 in annual revenue and $12,700 in annual profit.

At scale the potential annual profit to Tesla is impressive…

One million bots = $12.7 billion in profit
Ten million bots = $127 billion in profit
One hundred million bots = $1.27 trillion in profit
One billion bots = $12.7 trillion in profit

Applying an earnings multiple of 30 gives us a BOTS model what-if-value of $380,000 for each bot. At scale the potential BOTS value to Tesla is gigantic…

One million bots = $380 billion in added market value
Ten million bots = $3.8 trillion in added market value
One hundred million bots = $38 trillion in added market value
One billion bots = $380 trillion in added market value

At scale the annual tax receipts (ROBot tax + corporate income tax) to the government are rather substantial…

One million bots = $18 billion in taxes
Ten million bots = $180 billion in taxes
One hundred million bots = $1.8 trillion in taxes
One billion bots = $18 trillion in taxes

As a reference, in 2022 the US government collected just under $5 trillion in tax revenue. If there were 300 million bots working in the US they would generate $5.4 trillion in tax revenue!

Finally, from Elon, “I think we might exceed a one-to-one ratio of humanoid robots to humans. It's not even clear what an economy is at that point."

Yes. Assume it exists here. Australia does not have a special immunity to rorts, sloppy design, political slush funds or organised crime following a pile of public money. The scale is smaller than Washington, the language is politer, and the Auditor-General writes better reports — but the pattern is the same.

Both Labor and the Coalition have done it. The difference is usually which program is exploding this term, not whether the tap is dripping.

The big leaks (the ones that actually move the budget)

NDIS is the current champion. It was sold as insurance. It now costs about $50–53 billion a year and is forecast much higher. Officials have put “integrity leakage” — fraud, over-claiming, inappropriate payments, organised crime — at 6–10 per cent. That is $3–5 billion a year, and some internal briefings have suggested measurable losses may sit even higher. Payment-error testing showed provider and participant error rates climbing for years. There are hundreds of thousands of unregistered providers. The Fraud Fusion Taskforce has disrupted operators, executed warrants and seized assets. They are still chasing a firehose. A scheme this large with weak front-end controls was always going to attract professionals.

JobKeeper was the last decade’s prize. Roughly $89–101 billion. Analysis showed $13.8 billion (and estimates heading toward $20 billion) went to businesses whose turnover rose. Profitable listed companies paid dividends and kept the cash. Almost no clawback. That was not “keeping jobs.” That was a transfer from future taxpayers to firms that did not need it.

Grants and pork never died. Coalition: sports rorts, car parks. Labor in 2026: a $560 million community infrastructure program with about 73 per cent of the money landing in Labor-held or Labor-competitive seats. A golf club in the Prime Minister’s electorate copped millions. The Auditor-General is circling it. Same colour-coded logic, different team colours.

Consultants and the bureaucracy. Coalition capped the APS; Labor then grew it hard. Headcount went from around 150,000 near 2019–20 to nearly 199,000 by mid-2025; average staffing levels sit over 215,000. Consultant and labour-hire spend still runs into the hundreds of millions to billions. PwC leaked confidential tax policy to help clients dodge rules it helped write. KPMG had its own mess. You paid them to design the lock and then to sell the key.

Infrastructure blowouts. Defence sample work found $29 billion in cost growth before contracts were even signed. Snowy 2.0 started as a $2 billion announcement, became $12 billion, and is still climbing — some independent all-in estimates (plant, transmission, financing) go far higher. Victoria’s Big Build (North East Link, Suburban Rail Loop, Metro Tunnel and the rest) has seen original prices explode; North East Link went from about $15.6 billion toward $26 billion. Dozens of fraud, corruption and criminal-conduct allegations sit on federally co-funded Victorian projects. Extra labour costs from CFMEU practices and alleged organised-crime involvement are documented. Argue about the exact $15 billion figure if you like; the political protection and cost inflation are not a rumour.

Detected “fraud” looks tiny because most of it is never called fraud. The 2024–25 Commonwealth census recorded $110.7 million in reported external fraud losses and $2.4 million internal. GO Topeka is a private nonprofit contractor. JEDO is the public body. The law treats those two boards differently. Voters can hold both, but not with the same tool.

Two boards, two kinds of blame

JEDO members (mayor’s voting seat, Hiller, Cook as commissioner) are public officers. They vote the tax work order. Kansas ouster, cash-basis voidness, and misuse-of-public-funds analysis starts here.
GO Topeka directors (Perez, Duncan if they sit there, Cook in his second seat, Chamber people) are private fiduciaries spending a public grant. They are not “the City.” They do not automatically forfeit a public office when the nonprofit writes a bad check. Personal liability for a volunteer director in Kansas is narrow.
That split is the first thing a court will say. Do not write as if every banquet vote is a felony by the whole Chamber board. Write the stack.
What voters can do that is actually legal
1. Political.
Elect different JEDO votes. Demand the City and County terminate the service contract (audits: either party may terminate; cash and land revert to JEDO). Demand the GO Topeka board remove officers or stop the line. That is the Lawrence sequence you already described: show the problem, tell the voters, see if government moves.

2. Records and audit.
KORA on JEDO. Contract audit rights on GO Topeka. A 25-year total is how you prove pattern, which matters later for “willful.”
3. Recovery of the dollars.
Unauthorized payments can be demanded back from the contractor and, in a clean case, from the recipient. False Claims Act, K.S.A. 75-7503: knowing false claim for public money — treble damages to the political subdivision. That action runs against the person who presented the claim, not against every silent director.

4. Void the spend / end the contract.
If JEDO had no power to authorize that use, the payment is ultra vires. Genesis, Hecht, K.S.A. 10-1119. Ending C-2019-01 is a board vote plus notice, not a slogan.
5. Criminal — high bar.
K.S.A. 21-6005 (misuse of public funds) hits a custodian or other person who has control of public money by virtue of official position and knowingly uses it in a manner not authorized by law. Conviction forfeits the official position. That fits a public officer or a staffer who controlled the account. It is a harder fit for a volunteer nonprofit director who only voted “aye” on a lump budget, unless you can prove they knew the use was illegal and still permitted it. A 2019 Kansas case charged a nonprofit director who received public grants and spent them on personal travel and luxury items. That is theft of the grant, not a banquet-policy dispute.

6. Ouster — public officers only.
K.S.A. 60-1205: willful misconduct in office, willful neglect of a duty enjoined by law, or a penal offense involving moral turpitude. Kansas courts require corrupt purpose, habitual disregard, or a real threat to the public fisc — not one sloppy vote. State v. Morrison reversed an ouster that did not meet that bar. Quo warranto is brought in the name of the state, usually by the attorney general or county attorney. Private citizens do not oust a commissioner by Facebook post.
7. Private directors — fiduciary duty, not ouster.
Kansas K.S.A. 60-3601: if the nonprofit carries liability insurance, a volunteer director is not personally liable for ordinary mistakes. Liability opens on willful or wanton misconduct, or if that director authorizes, approves, or ratifies the act and the act is willful or wanton. The federal Volunteer Protection Act is the same idea. Business-judgment rule covers good-faith wrong guesses. It does not cover “we knew this was off the ballot and we kept signing.”

The Kansas Attorney General can enforce misuse of restricted funds against a charity. That is the usual path against a 501 board, not a voter lawsuit for damages against each director.
Kansas precedent that is close

Theis (2004), JEDO–GO Topeka: contract illegal for failure to bid; treated as void if the plaintiffs finished the case. They did not. JEDO passed a bid exemption. Lesson: the court will not kill the arrangement unless someone with standing completes the suit.
Hecht / Genesis / cash-basis cases: illegal municipal contracts are void; no estoppel; the other party is charged with knowledge. That is your best Kansas doctrine for the spend, not for sending directors to jail.

21-6005 + grant-funded nonprofit staff: personal use of grant money has been charged. Policy disagreement over “what is economic development” has not produced a reported Kansas ouster of an entire ED board.
There is no published Kansas case that says “the Chamber board is personally liable for every banquet paid from a sales-tax contract.” Do not invent one.

National pattern
Same split everywhere.
Public officials who vote illegal appropriations: some states allow a surcharge — personal repayment of the illegal item (North Carolina’s local-government literature is the clean write-up). Kansas does that work through voidness, recovery, and 21-6005, not a neat surcharge statute.

Nonprofit directors: personal liability when they loot, self-deal, or ignore a known illegal use. Ordinary program error stays on the corporation. D.C. and other AGs sue treasurers who took PTO money to Cancun. They do not sue the whole board for a sponsorship the staff buried in a program line.
Federal False Claims Act (and Kansas’s smaller cousin): the hammer when someone knowingly bills the government for something the contract did not allow.
Termination for convenience / for cause, clawback, debarment: how cities actually fire an ED contractor.

When the GO Topeka board “has to step up”
There is no calendar date that creates liability by itself. The legal turn is notice plus a later vote.
Before they were told the banquet was off the ballot: negligence argument, business judgment, volunteer immunity.

After letters, a KORA, a Howey list, and AG opinions are in their hands: the next “aye” on the same lump line is ratification. That is when 60-3601’s “authorizes, approves, ratifies” language starts to matter. That is when JEDO’s willful-neglect clock is easier to argue. That is when a prosecutor can say “knowingly.”
Justice, in this structure, is not a mass indictment of the Chamber. It is:
JEDO stops the line and splits incentives from sponsorships.
GO Topeka’s board orders staff to stop writing civic checks from the half-cent.

Unauthorized dollars come back.
If they refuse after notice, the City and County terminate C-2019-01 and take the cash and land.

Dual-role officers (Cook, and anyone else on both boards) get the harder questions because they had control and a law license.
Voters hold the public officers at the ballot and, with the AG or county attorney, in quo warranto. They hold the NGO board by forcing the public body to pull the contract and by putting ratification on the record after notice. That is the precedent. The letters you already sent are the notice that starts the second clock.
